 Election Day in Hawaii: Inside the final hours of in-person voting 
 Voters cast ballots at Honolulu Hale as officials urge those voting in person to be in line by the 7 p.m. cutoff. By HNN Staff Published : Nov. 3, 2026 at 5:50 PM HST | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Voters lined up at voter service centers across Hawaii Tuesday to cast their ballots on Election Day.
 Drop boxes will close at 7 p.m., however those who are in line to vote by 7 p.m. will be allowed to do so. An election worker will be positioned to mark the end of the line at the 7 p.m. cutoff.
 The first printout is expected shortly after the very last person has voted.
 View Election 2026 results here. 
 Voter lines Honolulu Hale (Hawaii News Now) At Honolulu Hale, light showers didn’t stop the steady flow of residents who showed up throughout the day.
 Voter Chelsea Lacolla said she’s “voting for the voiceless, people who may not be able to vote, like undocumented immigrants or animals and, you know, nature and earth,” she said. “I want to vote for that, to support everything good for the environment.”
 While lines remained manageable compared to the 2024 general election, election officials anticipate wait times will increase into the evening.
 “The staff is processing the people as they go through,” said Honolulu Elections Administrator Rex Quidilla. “The wait times haven’t been long, but there is still a line at all our service centers.”
 Voter lines at Kapolei Hale (Hawaii News Now) Our cameras were at Kapolei Hale early Tuesday morning before the voter service opened at 7 a.m. A crowd stood in line before the doors opened to get their ballots in before heading to work. 
 Election officials implemented operational adjustments following feedback from previous elections, including adding more staffing and creating expanded areas for voter sign-ups and indoor waiting.
 Nonpartisan election observers were also on site monitoring polling operations.
 Alphonso Braggs, Honolulu-Hawaii NAACP president, said the NAACP, in partnership with Common Cause, worked nationwide to ensure voters cast their ballots without interference.
 Braggs was at Kapolei Hale from 3 to 7 p.m.
 “I’ve seen elders. I’ve seen young folks. I’ve seen families come and witness what this process is really supposed to be about,” Braggs said. “The vote truly matters, and I’m very, very happy to see a lot of young people get involved and make sure that their voices are heard, their votes are counted.”
 Kauai votes for new mayor, county representatives
 Over on Kauai, residents were getting ready to vote for not only a new mayor, but seven new county council representatives.
 Many voters showed up in person, with a steady flow dropping off their ballots or walking in.
 “I would prefer going to the polls, personally. I understand the mail-in and appreciate it. I know that hopefully, we get more people to do it. But I prefer to do it the day of. I’m more of, I guess, a traditionalist. In many ways, I guess you can say,” said Fr. EJ Resinto.
 Some residents said they’re looking for change from their candidates.
 “Most of it is change, of course, I think everybody else thinks, you know, Mel has he’s been in the council for a long time, hasn’t been our mayor. So change up for the mayor. Hopefully he gives us a gun range and then Republican, mostly just because we’ve been under democratic control for so long,” said Sherry Rapozo.
